question: A Magento module keeps a cache of the current customer's cart in a class registered as a shared instance. You port the class to ASP.NET Core and register it with `AddSingleton`. What happens?
options: ASP.NET Core creates one singleton per request scope, so each customer keeps a separate cart
All concurrent requests share one instance until the process stops, so carts leak
The container creates one instance per thread, so carts mix only when two requests share a thread
The instance is shared, but ASP.NET Core resets its fields at the end of every request
explanation: An ASP.NET Core app is one long-running process, so a singleton lives until the process stops and every request gets the same instance. In Magento the shared instance only looked per-request because PHP-FPM discards everything after each request. The first option describes the scoped lifetime (module 05), which you must ask for explicitly; `AddSingleton` never behaves that way.

question: A Magento observer adds a security header to every HTTP response. Where does that behaviour belong in an ASP.NET Core app?
options: A `BackgroundService` that inspects each response after it is sent
An Options class bound from `appsettings.json` with the header values
Middleware in the request pipeline, registered in `Program.cs`
A singleton service that the container calls after every endpoint
explanation: Cross-cutting request behaviour that Magento puts in plugins and observers becomes middleware (or endpoint filters) in ASP.NET Core, added to the pipeline in `Program.cs`. The container only creates what something asks for; it never calls a registered service on its own, so the last option would do nothing. A `BackgroundService` runs outside the request and cannot change a response.

question: In PHP without `declare(strict_types=1)`, passing `"10"` to a function that declares `int` works. What happens with the same call in C#?
options: It compiles, and the call throws `InvalidCastException` at run time
It compiles, because C# coerces numeric strings unless strict mode is on
It compiles with a warning, and the string is parsed with `int.Parse`
The build fails: `string` does not convert implicitly to `int`
explanation: C# checks types at compile time, so the mismatch is reported (CS1503) before the program can run, and there is no per-file strict mode. The first option is the PHP strict-mode model, where a `TypeError` appears only when the call executes; in C# the call never gets that far.

question: Where do you register a service such as `TimeProvider` in a new ASP.NET Core web project?
options: In `Program.cs`, with `builder.Services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System)`
In `appsettings.json`, under a `Services` section the host reads at startup
Nowhere: the container creates any public class on request, like the ObjectManager
With an `[Injectable]` attribute on the class, which the host scans at startup
explanation: Composition in .NET is explicit C# code on `builder.Services`, read top to bottom; there is no XML merge and no attribute scanning by default. The third option is tempting for a Magento developer because the ObjectManager can create almost any class, but the .NET container only resolves what was registered.

question: An endpoint calls `File.ReadAllTextAsync(path).Result`. The code works on your laptop but the API slows down badly under load in production. Why?
options: `.Result` makes every request wait on one shared synchronization context
Each blocked call holds a pool thread while waiting, so the pool starves
Async file APIs are slower than sync ones, so `File.ReadAllText` would fix it
The file is read again on every call; it should be cached in a static field
explanation: Blocking on a task keeps a shared thread busy doing nothing; with many concurrent requests the pool runs out of threads and requests queue. `await` releases the thread while the I/O runs. Switching to the synchronous API, the third option, still blocks a thread per request and does not fix the starvation; ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, which rules out the first.

question: You find a C# answer online that uses a `Startup` class, `System.Web` and `web.config`. What should you conclude first?
options: It is the recommended structure for new .NET 10 APIs
It is current, but only for apps hosted in IIS rather than Kestrel
It was written for .NET Framework or early ASP.NET Core
It needs `<LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>` to compile on .NET 10
explanation: `System.Web` and `web.config` belong to .NET Framework, and a `Startup` class is the pre-.NET 6 ASP.NET Core pattern; current templates use top-level statements in `Program.cs`. The second option is tempting because `web.config` still appears when modern apps run behind IIS, but there it only configures the IIS module, and `System.Web` does not exist in modern .NET.
